Article Title: Asian Games Medal Tally: India win 8 medals but remain outside top 10 as gold continues to elude
Article Text:
Yashvir Singh, Rohit Yadav, and Esha Singh

Eight medals, but no gold for India

Shooting and kurash add to India's tally

NEW DELHI: India produced another strong medal haul at the Asian Games 2026 on Monday, winning eight medals across athletics, shooting and kurash. However, the impressive collection did not bring any change in the overall standings, with India remaining 12th as the country continued to wait for another gold medal.India added four silver and four bronze medals during the day but could not increase its gold tally. After Day 9, India stood at 45 medals — four gold, 20 silver and 21 bronze.'The eight-medal haul included silver medals for Yashvir Singh, Murali Sreeshankar, Gulveer Singh and Esha Singh, while Rohit Yadav, Parul Chaudhary, Vithya Ramraj and Pincky Balhara won bronze.India's strongest showing came in the men's javelin, where Yashvir and Rohit produced a double podium finish in the absence of defending champion Neeraj Chopra.Yashvir recorded a personal best of 85.72m for silver, while Rohit won bronze with 84.35m. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage claimed gold with 88.55m.Sreeshankar also won silver in the men's long jump with 8.07m despite an injury forcing him to abandon his final two attempts. China's Yuhao Shi took gold with 8.17m.Gulveer added his second silver of the Games with a personal best of 3:36.72 in the men's 1500m, having earlier finished runner-up in the 10,000m.Parul Chaudhary won bronze in the women's 5000m with 15:14.61, adding to the bronze she had claimed in the 3000m steeplechase.Vithya Ramraj also took bronze in the women's 400m hurdles with a personal best of 54.75 seconds.Esha Singh secured silver in the women's 25m pistol after finishing with 38 hits, the same score as China's Xiao Jiaruixuan, who won the gold after the shoot-off.Pincky Balhara added bronze in the women's -78kg kurash category, losing 0-5 to South Korea's Sumin Mo in the semifinals.Despite the eight medals, India's gold tally remained at four, a crucial factor in the standings as countries are ranked by gold medals first.China led with 132 golds, followed by Japan with 41, South Korea with 21 and Uzbekistan with 12. India remained 12th with 45 medals, highlighting how a large haul of silver and bronze medals has yet to translate into a significant rise in the standings.
Article Summary: India added four silver and four bronze medals during the day but could not increase its gold tally. After Day 9, India stood at 45 medals — four gold, 20 silver and 21 bronze. The eight-medal haul included silver medals for Yashvir Singh, Murali Sreeshankar, Gulveer Singh and Esha Singh.

One of the enduring memories of the Mamata Banerjee era in West Bengal will be the elaborate Durga Puja carnival, where handpicked(marquee pujas) would parade along Red Road with tableaux before the CM and other dignitaries in an almost Republic Day-esque procession. It would often end with Mamata Banerjee doing an impromptu jig with the crème de la crème of the Bengali film industry.The carnival has been scrapped. Instead, a pre-Puja event will be held at the iconic Eden Gardens on Mahalaya, October 10, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend. These and many other changes are expected as West Bengal counts down to the homecoming of the Goddess.This year marks a significant break in Bengal's politics. The BJP government took office on May 9, making this its first Durga Puja in power in the state. And some changes are already in motion. Beyond the cosmetic, is Bengal's intrinsic style of celebrating Durga Puja going to change?The number of pujas continues to grow. As of September 24, 2,318 Durga Pujas had already registered on Kolkata's Sahaj single-window permission portal, including 270 new applicants, with more applications still expected. In 2025, the final tally of 2,936 applications was the highest ever. Across Bengal, the state power department expects the number of community pujas to cross 65,000 this year, an estimate based partly on demand for temporary electricity connections.The, or community-puja, tradition in Bengal is generally traced to late-18th-century Guptipara, although historians differ over the precise year and even whether the earliest community celebration there was Durga Puja or Jagaddhatri Puja. The wordis generally traced to, or "twelve friends". From the patronage of zamindars to that of influential political leaders, Durga Puja's format has constantly changed, though it remains the cornerstone of Bengal's annual cultural calendar.From, where the divine family is presented within a single frame, to multi-part installations; from, or traditional-style idols, to theme pujas; fromto idols made from unconventional materials, creative people have continually found new ways to express their love and reverence for Goddess Durga.In the run-up to Mahalaya, Kumartuli, north Kolkata's famous idol-making quarter, draws growing crowds of photographers, selfie-seekers and curious visitors into its narrow lanes. The adjoining Kumartuli Ghat is now adding another attraction. A Rs 10-crore redevelopment of a 300-metre stretch of the Hooghly riverfront, with viewing areas, walkways and improved public facilities, is expected to add to the draw.The most visible change this year is in the patronage of Durga Pujas. For years, the names of influential Trinamool leaders were virtually interchangeable with those of Kolkata's marquee pujas. There was Sujit Bose's Sreebhumi, Arup Biswas's Suruchi, Firhad Hakim's Chetla Agrani and Partha Chatterjee's Naktala Udayan Sangha, among others.Along with these, many up-and-coming political leaders ensured that relatively unknown Durga pandals shot to fame with innovative themes. Often, hosting a large-scale Durga Puja became a proxy for growing political clout.That competition for spectacle and social ownership, however, long predates contemporary party politics. Kaliprasanna Sinha's 19th-century Hutom Pyanchar Naksha used Durga Puja to lampoon Calcutta's babu culture, its display, extravagance and social pretensions.At Sreebhumi Sporting Club, the extravaganza that became synonymous with former Trinamool minister Sujit Bose is being prepared by a new committee. BJP leader Kanak Debnath has become president, with the organisers promising to retain the puja's grandeur while ending prolonged road blockades.At Suruchi Sangha, for years associated with Arup Biswas and his brother Swarup, BJP MLA Sourav Sikdar is now secretary. Suruchi's new committee has replaced the Biswas brothers, although the transition was accompanied by protests from residents. At Tala Prattoy, which has been delivering extremely eye-catching themes over the last few years, much of the previous organising set-up has changed, with Sushanta Shibani Pal handling this year's theme.The organisational change is extending beyond individual clubs. A new statewide coordination platform, Paschim Banga Durga Puja Samannay Samiti, or West Bengal Durga Puja Coordination Committee, is taking shape, with Kartik Maharaj as chairman and BJP MLA Rudranil Ghosh as chief adviser. It could emerge as an alternative pole to the established Forum for Durgotsab, which represents hundreds of committees.The churn has reached venues old and new. Known for its elaborate Christmas and New Year celebrations, Park Street will host a Durga Puja at Allen Park for the first time this year. Without missing a beat, Kolkata Sanatani Sangha, fronted by BJP leader Shankudeb Panda, will be organising it.At Mohammad Ali Park, competing committees put up banners under different names after BJP councillor Meena Devi Purohit proposed renaming the historic venue Mahabali Park. The iconic Bagbazar Puja, meanwhile, landed in trouble over a deadlocked committee election before the courts sorted it out.The financial machinery behind Durga Puja is also being recalibrated. The Mamata Banerjee government introduced annual assistance to puja committees at Rs 10,000 in 2018 and increased it over the years to Rs 1.1 lakh in 2025. The new BJP government has announced Rs 1 lakh for 2026, while chief minister Suvendu Adhikari has appealed to big-budget organisers to leave the assistance for smaller celebrations that need it.During TMC rule, BJP leader Sajal Ghosh's Santosh Mitra Square was something of a 'rebel' puja, refusing to take grants. With power having changed hands and TMC virtually disintegrating, there are no such rebel pujas this time, at least publicly.Several prominent committees have agreed to forgo the grant, in line with the government's appeal. The BJP government has also asked electricity suppliers to provide free power to organisers; under the previous government, the waiver in 2025 was 80%.In Birbhum, BJP district president Uday Shankar Banerjee told puja committees that clubs taking the 2026 government grant must display the chief minister's photograph or face action, a claim promptly shot down by minister Dilip Ghosh.It is perhaps on food that the focus will be most intense.In late August, Swami Nirgunananda, a member of the VHP's central advisory council, suggested that non-vegetarian food should be kept away from the immediate puja space, while acknowledging that Bengal's Durga Puja has never been exclusively vegetarian. VHP leaders subsequently clarified that there was no official or binding directive banning non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja.Days later, religious preacher Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, popularly known as Bageshwar Baba, went considerably further. He criticised the consumption of non-vegetarian food during Durga Puja, describing those who did so as, or hypocrites.The remarks provoked criticism, including from within the BJP. State party president Samik Bhattacharya defended Bengal's food traditions, while Adhikari subsequently visited Kalighat temple and consumed traditional prasad that included fried fish, fish head and basanti pulao. At Suruchi Sangha, where BJP MLA Sourav Sikdar is now secretary, organisers have said mutton and hilsa will continue to be served at the Maha Navami feast. Many housing societies where community Durga Pujas take place have also affirmed that their Puja feasts aren't going to change and will remain largely non-vegetarian, barring Maha Ashtami.In large parts of north India, abstaining from meat during Navratri is commonplace. Critics of the BJP have expressed concern that such a food culture could gradually be pushed on Bengal. There is no evidence of any government plan to impose such a restriction. But the effect could be subtler than a formal ban.Some organisers are already drawing a firmer boundary around the immediate sacred space. Thakurpukur SB Park and Chaltabagan have announced restrictions on visitors entering while eating, while the new Allen Park puja will have no food stalls inside the park, TOI has reported previously.There is a perception that, at many pandals, egg-roll stalls and other non-vegetarian food outlets will be stationed farther away from the main arena where the Goddess will be placed.Theme pujas have not been barred, but organisers have been asked to ensure that idols and themes do not hurt religious sentiments or undermine what the new government describes as Sanatani traditions. That has prompted some artists and organisers to tread more cautiously.However, social and experimental subjects continue this year too, including themes around care workers, gender identity and ecology. What is changing is the political vocabulary surrounding them. At the same time, several high-profile pujas this year are invoking patriotism, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity.There is no official census separating theme pujas from traditional ones.Santosh Mitra Square, whose committee is headed by BJP MLA Sajal Ghosh, has chosen. New Town Sanatani Durga Puja, whose leadership includes chief ministerial adviser Subrata Gupta and Kartik Maharaj, is exploring what its organisers describe as the relationship between ancient Indian traditions and modern science.The use of Goddess Durga as a political or nationalist metaphor is hardly new. In Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay's(My Durga Puja), included in, an opium-addled Kamalakanta looks at the Durga image on Saptami and eventually sees in her Bengal itself (, Mother Bengal), invoking the Goddess as an image of collective strength and awakening.Nazrul would later take the idea in another direction. In his Durga and Agomoni compositions, the rebel poet repeatedly invoked the Goddess as Shakti, or living power, rather than merely an image of clay. His 1922 poemused Durga's arrival as an anti-colonial metaphor so explicitly that the British prosecuted him for sedition The VHP's Nirgunananda, though, has argued for a more explicitly religious ownership of the festival. At an August meeting with Puja organisers, he rejected the formulation that "religion belongs to individuals, but festivals belong to everyone", arguing instead that festivals primarily belong to followers of the faith, while people of other religions were welcome to visit.That marks a clear difference in outlook, which may well become one of the faultlines around Bengal's Durga Puja celebrations.Pandal-hopping has also traditionally been an easy way to get a crash course in political history.The Left Front's stalls, where thewould be stationed selling books on, or Marxist philosophy, were hard to miss. Seeing them, the TMC also started its Jago Bangla stalls, though Didi, a skilled politician, never quite got the stamp of approval from Bengalis for her literary exploits.This year, though, the Left may face problems putting up some of those stalls.The name, synonymous with Durga Puja, is facing questions. Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari has asked committees not to accommodate CPI(M) bookstalls that describe the festival as "Sharadotsav" instead of "Durga Puja", arguing that the terminology dilutes its religious identity.Interestingly, Rabindranath Tagore wrote, a play celebrating the autumn season, way back in 1908, a point also raised by Left leaders in response to the controversy. A puja committee at Kamardanga in Tangra has gone further, announcing that it will not allow stalls run by CPI(M), DYFI, SUCI or other Left-wing organisations at its celebration. The committee has appealed to other organisers to follow suit, while CPI(M) has criticised the move.The Red Road immersion carnival, first held under Mamata Banerjee's government in 2016, has been discontinued. In its place comes a grand Mahalaya celebration at Eden Gardens on October 10, 2026, one week before Maha Shashthi on October 17. The programme is expected to feature traditional performers, thousands of dhakis, fireworks and a drone show. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to attend and virtually inaugurate prominent Kolkata pujas from the programme. The Eden Gardens presentation aims to recreate important events and rituals associated with Durga Puja.Mahalaya holds a very special significance. Beyond, the ritual offering to one's ancestors, Birendra Krishna Bhadra's recitation in theradio programme, which became associated with Mahalaya from the 1930s, has itself become a ritual. Hosting such a gala event on that day gives the new government a prominent ceremonial role at the opening of Bengal's Puja season.There are changes for ordinary pandal-hoppers too. The new government has said Puja pandals will not be allowed to be inaugurated before Mahalaya. Maha Ashtami will be a dry day, with liquor sales prohibited. DJs have been banned during Puja celebrations and immersion processions, while organisers have been instructed to avoid prolonged road blockades and complete immersions within the prescribed period.Even the appearance of Kolkata Police's crowd-management volunteers is set to change, with police floating a tender for orange T-shirts and caps to replace the familiar white-and-blue attire.There is not much clarity yet about how active the TMC will be during Durga Puja. But one thing Kolkata will surely be revisiting through reels is Mamata Banerjee's one-liners and gestures, from her suggestion that, the tall white kans grass associated with the Bengali autumn, could be used as stuffing for pillows to her symbolicSo will Bengal's intrinsic style of celebrating Puja change? The answer may lie in how varied that style has always been.There has never been one compulsory Bengali Puja menu, or even one compulsory visual grammar. Mahendranath Datta, the younger brother of Swami Vivekananda, recorded striking differences between Durga images in Shakta and Vaishnava households . In Shakta homes, he wrote, Durga's lion had the conventional lion's face; in Gosain or Vaishnava homes, the lion had a horse-like face, apparently marking a distinction between the two traditions. On food too, practices differed. At Brahmin homes, guests could be served rice, five vegetable dishes, curd and payesh; in Shakta Brahmin households, he noted, fish was also permitted, while Kayastha homes served luchi.The traditions that have survived in Bengal's old family pujas are equally difficult to squeeze into a single dietary rule. The Sabarna Roy Chowdhury family continues to offer katla as Nabami bhog.At Chorbagan Chatterjee Bari, fish is offered during the Puja days. At the Janbazar home of Rani Rashmoni's descendants, on the other hand, the Goddess receives vegetarian bhog even as non-vegetarian food is served to guests, reported TOI previously.There is no quick primer on how to be Sanatani across Bengal's myriad Durga Puja traditions. The pandals may change hands, and the colour of uniforms may change. But beneath the contest for ownership lies a diversity of practice too old and too deep-rooted.Perhaps the more things change, the more they stay the same.
Article Summary: This year marks a significant break in Bengal's politics. The BJP government took office on May 9, making this its first Durga Puja in power in the state. The carnival has been scrapped. Instead, a pre-Puja event will be held at the iconic Eden Gardens on Mahalaya.

Article Title: ​In a first, government admits in SC problem of exorbitant pricing of drugs, promises fix
Article Text:
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said there was no rationale for controlling the price of a few scheduled medicines and allowing the rest to be sold at inflated prices as all medicines are essential. It suggested a uniform rule limiting the MRP to not more than 16% above the price to the retailer (PTR).

NEW DELHI: With Supreme Court toughening its stand against poor patients being forced to pay exorbitant prices for medicines, govt on Tuesday admitted that there was a problem and assured the court it would make efforts to address it.A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said there was no rationale for controlling the price of a few scheduled medicines and allowing the rest to be sold at inflated prices as all medicines are essential. It suggested a uniform rule limiting the MRP to not more than 16% above the price to the retailer (PTR).SG Tushar Mehta told SC that he had discussed the issue with official concerned. Govt was not taking an adversarial stand on it, he said, seeking time for further consultations to find a solution. “We will have to find a way out. Some way that balances equities... let me sit with officers and then respond,” he said.The court said taxpayers’ money was also wasted because of exorbitant medicine prices as corporate hospitals obtain full reimbursement for inflated MRPs when patients undergo treatment under govt-sponsored welfare schemes, with the money being paid from the exchequer.“It affects society. Pharma companies are not bothered about it. Why do they fix MRP at high prices? This is carnage... Corporate hospitals are not going to spare anyone, and they will charge the price at MRP. Why should common man suffer like this?” SC asked.After the hearing, the SC adjourned the case for Oct 12.
Article Summary: A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said there was no rationale for controlling the price of a few scheduled medicines. It suggested a uniform rule limiting the MRP to not more than 16% above the price to the retailer (PTR)

Article Title: IISc team uses blue light to switch on cell division; may aid cancer research
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Scientists from IISc ’s Department of Microbiology and Cell Biology (MCB) have found a way to use blue light to switch on a key part of the machinery that helps cells divide, and have used it to restore cell division in cells from which a crucial structure had been removed.The finding could help scientists understand how cells divide and, eventually, identify new targets for drugs against diseases such as cancer. The study has been published in EMBO Reports. And their new technique may also help further cancer researchCell division is a tightly controlled process. Before a cell splits into two, its genetic material has to be copied and then pulled apart accurately. This is done by the mitotic spindle, a network of thread-like structures that attaches to the genetic material and separates it.The centrosome, a small structure inside the cell, helps organise this spindle. It’s made up of more than 200 components, but which are essential has remained unclear..The IISc team has developed a technique called Light-Induced Spindle Activation (LISA), which allows them to switch on Aurora A, an enzyme involved in building the spindle, by shining blue light on it.Aurora A normally becomes active at the centrosome, where it gathers into clusters.Scientists had believed that a protein called Cep192 was needed to help activate it. LISA showed that Aurora A can instead be artificially clustered and activated using light, without Cep192.Researchers adapted an existing technique called LARIAT, which uses light to make proteins cluster together. They attached Aurora A to a light-sensitive plant protein called CRY2 and introduced it into human cells.When blue light was shone on the cells, CRY2 interacted with another protein, CIB1, causing Aurora A molecules to cluster. This, in turn, triggered the formation of microtubules, the tiny structures that make up much of the spindle.“This provides a novel way to trigger and activate an artificial Aurora A kinase complex – Aurora A fused to light-sensitive plant proteins, which is sufficient to induce microtubule nucleation,” Vignesh Olakkal, a PhD student in Sachin Kotak’s lab and first author of the study, said.Researchers then asked whether the technique could actually compensate for a missing centrosome. They chemically removed centrosomes from human cells, which normally causes problems during cell division. They then introduced the light-controlled Aurora A system.When blue light was applied during cell division, Aurora A clustered and triggered the formation of microtubules. The cells were able to rebuild their spindles, effectively rescuing the division defects caused by the loss of centrosomes.The technique may also help in cancer research. Aurora A is overexpressed in many solid tumours and is already targeted by some drugs. But because the enzyme acts on several different proteins, it can be difficult to determine exactly which of its functions should be blocked.“In many solid tumours, Aurora A kinase is overexpressed, and that’s why there are drugs targeting it. But Aurora A kinase has multiple targets. Now, with our strategy, we can find out what the Aurora A kinase-specific targets are, independent of the centrosome, as far as microtubule nucleation is concerned. Then we will hopefully be able to find other targets of Aurora A kinase and design drugs,” Kotak said.
Article Summary: Scientists from IISc have found a way to use blue light to switch on a key part of the machinery that helps cells divide. They used it to restore cell division in cells from which a crucial structure had been removed. The finding could help scientists understand how cells divide and identify new targets for drugs against diseases such as cancer.

"It is stated in our ancient texts that Dharma stands on four pillars: the first is Truth, the second is Compassion, the third is Penance, and the fourth is Purity of thought and action, both internal and external," Bhagwat said.Yavatmal (Maharashtra) [India], September 29 (ANI): RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Tuesday emphasised that sustainable national progress must be rooted in the four essential pillars of Dharma—Truth (Satya), Compassion (Karuna), Penance (Tapascharya), and Purity (Antarbahya Pavitrata)—as exemplified by Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya's philosophy of Integral Humanism (Ekatma Manav Darshan).Speaking at an event organised to mark the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya Jayanti in Maharashtra's Yavatmal, Bhagwat noted that genuine social welfare demands upliftment starting from the most vulnerable sections through Antyodaya, rather than focusing solely on utilitarian metrics.Emphasising the foundational values governing human conduct, Bhagwat pointed out that Dharma transcends mere rituals or personal habits. Article Title: Cyber fraud can outwit the tech-savvy too, IIT study finds
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: A career in IT and security did not save her from losing Rs 90 lakh to cybercrime. The professional, with 28 years of experience, was among 33 victims interviewed for an IIT Madras-led study that found technological familiarity could be overwhelmed by fear, urgency and psychological manipulation.Participants came from Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, New Delhi and Mumbai; the sample included 12 senior citizens. Participants included bankers, doctors, IT professionals and people with cybersecurity certifications. One reported a loss of Rs 1.12 crore even after recovering Rs 25 lakh.Published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, the qualitative study explores how victims were deceived, rather than measuring national risk. Its urban, professionally employed sample cannot establish that educated people are more vulnerable than others.Many participants were navigating illness in the family, retirement, job searches or workplace pressure. Fraudsters exploited these circumstances through investment promises, employment offers or threats to reputation. Some victims sought quick returns; others paid because they feared arrest or harm to relatives.“The way they act and talk, you cannot believe that they are not police officers—they play a psychological game with you,” the IT and security professional said in the study.In “digital arrest” scams, victims described being confined to rooms, monitored over video and coached to mislead bank managers. A plastic surgeon said: “They emotionally manipulated and trapped me: every half an hour I had to send them pics that I am alone”.In task-based scams, criminals initially paid victims for simple online assignments to build trust, then pressed them to invest larger sums and borrow from relatives or friends when funds dwindled.The researchers also found neglected device updates and missing security software among participants. Their accounts suggest psychological manipulation can work alongside technical weaknesses. Some victims subsequently abandoned online payments and returned to cash.The damage extended beyond bank balances. Victims reported sleeplessness, shame and strained family relationships. Institutional responses were uneven: some banks helped, while others blamed customers; some victims reported being sent between police stations.The researchers call for awareness campaigns explaining specific fraud tactics, stronger police expertise, faster bank detection and better coordination between banks, police and courts. “The response to cybercrime must move beyond blaming victims,” said IIT Madras adjunct faculty member P Kandaswamy in a statement.
Article Summary: IIT Madras-led study found technological familiarity could be overwhelmed by fear, urgency and psychological manipulation. Participants included bankers, doctors, IT professionals and people with cybersecurity certifications. One reported a loss of Rs 1.12 crore even after recovering Rs 25 lakh.

Article Title: 'Look into her eyes': Neeru Dhanda's hospital scare, 2 Asian Games golds and the 'fire' Mansher Singh saw
Article Text:
Neeru Dhanda (Image credit: PTI)

‘Winning the World Cup and Asian Games in the same year is incredible’

Neeru Dhanda and Mansher Singh (Image credit: Special arrangement)

‘The Olympic medal is the first thing’

NEW DELHI: Neeru Dhanda does not need to be aggressive to show her competitive side. “Look into her eyes,” says Mansher Singh, her coach of seven years.The 25-year-old shooter on Tuesday became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games gold in trap, following her World Cup triumph in Italy in July. For Mansher, who has watched Neeru develop since she was 18, the performance was another expression of a quality he has seen throughout her career.“She has a lot of fire in her belly. If in the final, she will go all guns blazing and that’s what she did,” Mansher told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.Neeru shot 28 in the final in Aichi-Nagoya, surpassing the previous Asian record of 24. She had earlier won a silver medal in the women's trap team event at the Games.The Asian Games gold came less than three months after Neeru became the first Indian woman to win an individual World Cup gold in trap, at the Shotgun World Cup in Italy. At Aichi-Nagoya, after the individual gold, she claimed her second gold in the mixed team events to add to the silver she clicnhed in the women’s team trap event.“She is not aggressive at all. If you want to see the aggression, look into her eyes,” Mansher said.“I’m just proud and happy that she’s got what she deserves because she’s very hardworking and very determined to be successful and, more importantly, to achieve. She has achieved things which have not happened in the past.”Mansher believes the back-to-back titles have changed the conversation around his student.“So she wants to go to new heights, and this is exactly what she’s doing now. She’s won the last two big competitions. She’ll be the first Indian woman to do this, you know. So, winning the World Cup and Asian Games in the same year, almost back to back, is incredible,” he said.Neeru's rise has also been accompanied by a change in the way she handles the pressure around her.“She used to fight with me a lot. Then I would say, ‘I’m like your father.’ Then she would say, ‘Yes, I can’t fight with my father.’ Then she would come back to normal,” Mansher recalled.“But she was an emotional person. She’s much more mature now. She’s able to take her decisions and think about the consequences.”The coach was also closely involved when Neeru fell ill shortly before the Asian Games.She was admitted to PSRI Hospital in Chirag Delhi after a viral fever did not improve with medication. Even while on the hospital bed, Mansher said, Neeru remained focused on the competition ahead.“Sir, medal lana hai desh ke liye. This is all she had been saying while on the hospital bed. I was just happy and worried at the same time,” he recalled.Neeru was discharged and travelled to Japan without much time to recover.Mansher's message to her before she left was simple.“You should be happy that God has blessed you with the opportunity to go after being so sick for eight days that you were in hospital. Enjoy yourself and celebrate,” he told her.With the World Cup and Asian Games titles now secured in the same year, attention will turn to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.India's last Olympic shotgun medal came through Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore, who won silver in men's double trap at Athens 2004. Since then, India have not won an Olympic medal in shotgun.Mansher, who represented India at four Olympics - Los Angeles 1984, Atlanta 1996, Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008 - said the Olympic target has long been part of their conversations.“I think we don’t have to worry about that. She’s very centred. She knows that’s her goal. She’s not going to take a gold medal at the World Cup and at the Asian Games and make it so big that she loses sight of her ultimate goal,” Mansher said.“And it’s always been a conversation amongst us that, you know, the Olympic medal is the first thing. The Olympics are the first and last thing in this sport.”For Mansher, the two gold medals have provided something more useful than simply another set of titles.“But overall, there’s proof enough to say that you are definitely in that league or in that conversation to be a medalist at the Olympics,” he said.
Article Summary: Neeru Dhanda becomes first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games gold in trap. The 25-year-old shot 28 in the final in Aichi-Nagoya, surpassing the previous Asian record of 24. She had earlier won a silver medal in the women's trap team event at the Games.

Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar could soon move from being one of the Pakistan Cricket Board’s most vocal critics to having a role in shaping its cricketing decisions.Akhtar is reportedly in line for a major position within the PCB as chairman Mohsin Naqvi looks to restructure the board’s cricket think tank following Pakistan’s disastrous tour of England, PTI reported. While the exact nature of the proposed role has not been formally announced, Akhtar and Naqvi have already held discussions over Pakistan cricket.A source close to the PCB said Akhtar, who resides in Islamabad, met Naqvi last week and the two spoke at length about cricket-related matters.“Few weeks back when Shoaib’s elder brother passed away Mohsin Naqvi had interacted with him closely and was there for him. This gesture impressed Shoaib a lot who has been a vocal critic of the PCB and Pakistan cricket in the past in his media appearances,” the source added.The relationship between the two has since strengthened, with Naqvi also sharing his plans with Akhtar and inviting him to visit the National Cricket Academy (NCA) and training camps.“Shoaib is in line to get a major posting but obviously when he met with the Chairman he had his own set of ideas and conditions through which he believes Pakistan cricket can be taken forward,” the source said.Akhtar's potential appointment comes as the PCB considers changes beyond the senior men's team.The board is also exploring the possibility of bringing in foreign coaches and consultants following the departures of senior team fielding coach Shane McDermott and batting coach Ashley Noffke.The women's national team is another area under review, with the PCB considering the appointment of a permanent long-term head coach.“The board is working on some plans for the future and there will be some changes in the cricket think tank soon because the Chairman has made it clear that he expects better results from the national mens, womens, shaheens and junior teams,” the source stated.The proposed restructuring follows a difficult period for Pakistan cricket, particularly after the men's team's Test series in England.Pakistan were beaten 3-0 in the series, suffering a first-ever clean sweep in a Test series on English soil. The result has increased scrutiny on the national side as well as the wider cricketing structure surrounding it. In the middle of the series, Pakistan sent back seven players, including Mohammed Rizwan and Imam-ul-Haq, as well as head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and bowling coach Umar Gul. Mike Hesson was subsequently asked to fill the head coach role in the third Test.The PCB is therefore examining changes to its cricketing setup, including coaching and consultancy appointments, rather than restricting its response to the senior men's team.Akhtar has spent years speaking publicly about Pakistan cricket, regularly questioning selection decisions, administrative choices and the direction of the national team. His outspoken views have often made him a prominent critic of the PCB.A formal role within the board would therefore mark a significant change for the former fast bowler. Instead of analysing Pakistan cricket from outside the system, Akhtar could potentially have a direct say in the decisions and plans he has frequently commented on.The precise position being considered for him, however, is yet to be formally announced.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan fast bowler Shoaib Akhtar could soon move from being one of the Pakistan Cricket Board's most vocal critics to having a role in shaping its cricketing decisions. Akhtar is reportedly in line for a major position within the PCB as chairman Mohsin Naqvi looks to restructure the board’s cricket think tank. The exact nature of the proposed role has not been formally announced.

Article Title: To end 34-year Ranji drought, Punjab rope in 38-year-old Umesh Yadav as guest player | Exclusive

NEW DELHI: Punjab are turning to experience in its quest to end a 34-year wait for the Ranji Trophy, making a significant departure from their traditional approach by signing 38-year-old India pacer Umesh Yadav as a guest player for the 2026-27 domestic season. The move is historic for the Punjab Cricket Association (PCA), with Umesh becoming the first guest player signed by the association.Umesh, who has played 55 Tests, 75 ODIs and nine T20Is for India, has received a no-objection certificate (NOC) from the Vidarbha Cricket Association (VCA) and will play for Punjab this season. PCA president Amarjit Mehta confirmed the veteran pacer's move from Vidarbha to Punjab."He has proven credentials as a bowler. He has won the Ranji Trophy with Vidarbha and has been a champion bowler for India as well," Mehta told TimesofIndia.com.Asked about the decision to sign a player who will turn 39 in three weeks, and about the historic nature of the move, Mehta said: "We have taken the decision keeping our red-ball cricket in focus. Punjab have not won the Ranji Trophy since 1992 and we think Umesh is someone who can deliver us the title."His experience is going to be invaluable to the youngsters in the team. There is so much to learn from someone of Umesh's stature."Mehta also pointed to Punjab's fast-bowling resources being stretched, with Gurnoor Brar and Arshdeep Singh expected to be away on India duty."Look, our boys, whenever they are available, play for Punjab. But Gurnoor and Arshdeep will be busy with India duty, and with them gone, our bowling becomes weak. This is also one of the reasons why we have decided to bring in Umesh Yadav," he said.Umesh, who last played for India in the World Test Championship (WTC) final against Australia at The Oval in June 2023, is likely to join the Punjab Ranji Trophy camp in the next day or two."He is still fit and, in Indian conditions, along with Mohammed Shami , Umesh was lethal. I think age is just a number and Umesh ticks all the boxes when it comes to fitness," Punjab coach Amit Uniyal told this website."Having said that, there is no guarantee that he will play all the matches. A lot will depend on the combination as well. But his presence in the dressing room is going to be huge," he added.Punjab will play their first game of the Ranji Trophy season against Assam at New Chandigarh from October 11.
Article Summary: Punjab sign 38-year-old Umesh Yadav as a guest player for 2026-27 domestic season. Yadav has played 55 Tests, 75 ODIs and nine T20Is for India. Punjab have not won the Ranji Trophy since 1992.

Article Title: Gulveer Singh completes Asian Games medal treble after gruelling five-day athletics test
Article Text:
India's Gulveer Singh (AP/PTI)

Pooja jumps to bronze

Bronze in mixed relay

Nagoya: Before leaving for training or competitions, Gulveer Singh has a ritual he never skips. He prays to a small statue of Lord Hanuman that he carries with him everywhere and applies vermilion to his forehead.By the time he completed his 5000m race on Tuesday night, the red mark between his brows had long been washed away by rain and sweat. But the 29-year-old had left an indelible mark on the Asian Games, completing a treble of medals: a bronze in the 5000m to go with silvers in the 10,000m and 1500m.His week at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium has been defined by perseverance, discipline and versatility. Built on a staple diet of daal, roti, sabzi, paneer and protein supplements, his lean frame has carried him through three gruelling races in five days, producing a feat rarely seen in Indian athletics.Gulveer clocked a personal best of 13:32.75 to finish behind Bahrain’s Birhanu Balew (13:30.79) and Japan’s Tomonori Yamaguchi (13:31.43).The three-medal haul, he said, was the result of sticking religiously to his routines and his coach’s plans.“I set out with the target of wanting to win three medals and I’m happy to have achieved that. I just listen to what the coach tells me and follow his plans. I never say, ‘Today I won’t do this.’I follow the coach completely,” Gulveer said.Meanwhile, 3000m steeplechaser Avinash Sable , who finished fourth in his pet event, did not start.For a while, Pooja’s name at the top of the high-jump leaderboard offered the possibility of a golden leap. The 19-year-old, however, had to settle for bronze after clearing 1.84m.The national record holder was flawless through 1.70m, 1.75m, 1.80m and 1.84m, clearing each height on her first attempt. She then failed all three attempts at 1.87m, but her clean card at 1.84m was enough to earn her the final podium spot on countback.Harita Bhadra, a last-minute inclusion in the squad, justified her selection by anchoring India to bronze in the mixed 4x100m relay.The quartet of Gurindervir Singh, Sneha Satyanarayana, Animesh Kujur and Harita timed a season-best 41.06 seconds.India were fourth heading into the final leg, but Harita, who won bronze in the 200m earlier in the Games, produced a strong finish to overtake Sri Lanka’s Shanthi Perera and bring India another bronze.China won gold in 40.78 seconds, while Thailand took silver in 40.87.India signed off their athletics campaign with one gold, nine silver and 14 bronze.
Article Summary: Gulveer Singh won a bronze in the 5000m to go with silvers in the 10,000m and 1500m. The 29-year-old clocked a personal best of 13:32.75 to finish behind Bahrain's Birhanu Balew and Japan's Tomonori Yamaguchi. Pooja jumped to bronze after clearing 1.84m.

Article Title: Delhi records coolest September morning for second time
Article Text:
The minimum is forecast to hover between 20°C and 22°C over the next two days.





NEW DELHI: The city experienced its coolest morning for the second time this month, with the minimum temperature dropping to 21 degrees Celsius, two notches below normal, at its base station Safdarjung Tuesday.Ridge observatory in north Delhi was cooler, recording Delhi’s lowest minimum at 16.9°C, six notches below normal.The mercury in Safdarjung had dropped to 21°C Sunday as well, making it the lowest minimum temperature recorded in Sept in the city in the past 18 years and the second lowest since 2001. “The lowest on record so far is 20.8°C on Sept 6, 2008,” said an IMD official.The minimum is forecast to hover between 20°C and 22°C over the next two days. The mean minimum temperature this Sept was 25.5°C, up from 24.8°C last Sept.The maximum Tuesday was 32.4°C, over two degrees below normal, up from 28.7°C a day earlier. It is likely to stay between 32 and 34°C Wednesday. The mean maximum temperature this Sept was 34°C, compared with 34.8°C last Sept.Delhi received 79.7 mm of rainfall this month, the lowest recorded in a Sept since 2020, when the city had got just 20.9 mm.This Sept ended with a rainfall deficit of 35.5%, against the entire month’s normal of 123.5 mm. Though there were six rainy days this Sept, only light to moderate showers were logged. There was no ‘heavy rainfall day’ this month.In contrast, Delhi received 136.1 mm rainfall in 2025, 192.5 mm in 2024, 82.7 mm in 2023, 164.5 mm in 2022 and 413.3 mm in 2021.Monsoon retreated from the city on Sept 23, two days before its normal date of withdrawal, with Safdarjung logging 728.6 mm rainfall over the season. Categorised as ‘normal’, it was 16% above the average of 629.7 mm. Last year, the city had recorded 41% surplus rainfall in monsoon.

Article Title: In 2022, 11 zoo workers rode out Hurricane Ian at Central Florida Zoo, staying around the clock so every animal continued to receive care through the storm
Article Text:
Entrance of Central Florida Zoo & Botanical Gardens alongside Hurricane Ian at peak intensity while approaching Florida. Credits - Wikipedia

Inside the ride-out crew

What

Hurricane Ian

did to Sanford

A green-winged macaw and a zoo worker in Central Florida Zoo & Botanical Gardens, Sanford, United States. Credits - Wikipedia

Why zoos plan like this

Poll Vote & Share your view Should zoos evacuate animals during hurricanes? Yes, they should evacuate No, keep them secure at the zoo 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

When a hurricane threatens a zoo, staff can choose whether to evacuate. The animals can't, and they still need food, warmth and veterinary care during a storm. Many zoos keep a small ride-out crew on site during storms. In September 2022, the Central Florida Zoo and Botanical Gardens in Sanford put that strategy to the test. According to the zoo , from Wednesday through Friday, a team of 11 animal care, veterinary and facility professionals from the Central Florida Zoo remained at the zoo 24 hours a day. The outcome was successful, all the animals and crew stayed safe, although the storm caused heavy damage around the grounds. The episode shows how preparation and a small on-site crew can protect animals during a hurricane.It was a team of mixed skills, and that counted. "Zookeepers fed and cared for the animals daily, veterinary staff stood by for any medical problems, and the facilities crew maintained the buildings and grounds. The zoo, home to more than 400 animals, closed to visitors on September 28, the day Ian made landfall on Florida's west coast.Preparation had begun days earlier. The animal care staff is getting additional food and medication and moving it to locations that won't flood," Christopher Torge, the zoo's head of animal operations, said ahead of the storm.The veterinary staff confirmed that zookeepers had all the medicines they would need, and the nutrition crew arranged meals to last several days. ABC News reported that the birds were kenneled and moved to a safe building where the crew would also shelter, with extra food, blankets and toys to keep them calm.The zoo said in its statement that all of its animals had safe, secure quarters to ride-out the storm and that every bird was brought indoors for extra protection. That routine work can make the difference between safety and disaster.Ian was a wild tempest even when far from where it initially made landfall. The National Hurricane Cente r said it made landfall in southwestern Florida as a Category 4 hurricane and caused record freshwater flooding across much of central and northern Florida. Its assessment says Ian damaged 1,656 structures in Seminole County, home of the zoo, and more than 250 water rescues in central and eastern Florida.Zoo officials who walked the grounds Friday found fallen trees, damaged fences, two buildings with water damage and debris in the walkways. The Wayne M. Densch Discovery Center suffered the worst damage, with water bubbling up from bathroom drains and storm water forcing its way into the back of the building. Repairs were estimated to take a month or more.The greater surprise came days later. Stormwater flowed towards Lake Monroe and started rising rapidly Sunday night, and by Monday morning the only road in and out of the zoo was overflowing. That morning, managers sent non-essential staff and volunteers home and devised a plan to ferry essential workers in and out each day to tend to the animals, including a second ride-out team if one became necessary. From then on, Glover said, staff were on site every day, even when the water made the road impassable. The zoo reopened on October 26 after a four-week closure, and CEO Richard Glover estimated damage and operating costs at more than $800,000.The vast majority of zoos do not evacuate their animals, and there are good reasons for this. Because hurricanes can change direction at the last minute, transferring animals can mean driving them right into a more dangerous spot, Zoo Miami explained. The stress of transit can be more dangerous than staying in a secure building during the storm. The safer way is to bolster the housing and keep the people with the animals.Past calamities have also helped shape planning. A US Department of Agriculture gap analysis of zoo and aquarium resilience in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 revealed that facilities with pre-catastrophe action plans did better and recovered more, according to the AZA, the Association of Zoos and Aquariums Other zoos do things that way. In Houston, the Houston Zoo had 15 team members on site the first night of Hurricane Harvey, sleeping on cots on the floor and using radios to ensure every animal had the correct feed, NPR reported. At Central Florida Zoo, staff also faced damage and losses at home but put the animals first, CEO Richard Glover said in an October 7 note. That part of the story is harder to capture in a checklist.The Sanford example shows how ride-out crews work in practice. The flooding that followed kept the zoo closed, but every animal stayed safe. Storms can only be anticipated so far, which is why zoos rely on preparation and a small crew willing to stay.
Article Summary: The Central Florida Zoo and Botanical Gardens in Sanford put that strategy to the test. A team of 11 animal care, veterinary and facility professionals remained at the zoo 24 hours a day. The outcome was successful, all the animals and crew stayed safe, although the storm caused heavy damage around the grounds.

How the fire came to the neighbourhood

Why some homes did not burn
